results.title: A goal-based weighting for composite indicators constructed through Ordered Weighted Averaging (OWA) operator - PMC
results.content: # A goal-based weighting for composite indicators constructed through Ordered Weighted Averaging (OWA) operator. The Ordered Weighted Averaging (OWA) operator is a multicriteria method that has conquered space among researchers in the composite indicators field. This paper introduces a method that defines the weights of the OWA operator based on two quality parameters of the composite indicator: the ability to capture the concept of the multidimensional phenomenon and the informational loss. In contrast, the Data Envelopment Analysis, Benefit of the Doubt, and Ordered Weighted Averaging (OWA) methods consider that sub-indicators can influence the scores of decision-making units at different intensities . ## Ordered Weighted Averaging (OWA) operator in composite indicators. The OWA operator was proposed by Yager as a method of aggregating weighted ordered information that has gained more and more space among researchers in the composite indicators field , , , . Table 2 also shows a difference of 0.39 in the average score of the composite indicator of public goods constructed with weighted sub-indicators with equal weights and weights defined by the Goal-based OWA operator. The maps in Fig. 4 allow to visualize this effect through the Goal-based OWA composite indicator scores and their difference from the Equal Weights, PCA, and BoD composite indicators. The other maps reveal that data-driven weighting (PCA and BoD) increases the differences between scores, and that there are positive and negative differences between the scores of the composite indicators constructed by Goal-based OWA and Equal Weights. The average variation between the rankings of the decision-making units of the Goal-based OWA and BoD composite indicators is 18.81 positions. The uncertainty between the rankings of the decision-making units of the composite indicators constructed by the Goal-based OWA and the SAW and PCA can be considered low. results.title: Comprehensive weighting method: Significance and symbolism
results.content: Comprehensive weighting method is a strategy used to assign importance to different risk indicators by combining various approaches. Comprehensive weighting method combines expert opinions and data analysis to assign importance to risk indicators. (1) The comprehensive weighting method combines different weighting approaches to minimize deviations and improve the reliability of the overall assessment. (2) The traditional combination weighting method achieves a reasonable distribution of subjective and objective weights, only makes the weights uniform, and weakens the difference between the main evaluation index and the secondary evaluation index. (3) A comprehensive weighting method is used to evaluate port logistics competitiveness, showing a quantitative approach to assessing port performance. (4) The comprehensive weighting method, based on IGT, optimizes the subjective and objective weighting values obtained by AHP and PCA methods, creating a more balanced evaluation. (5) The comprehensive weighting method seeks consistency between various weight sets and retains the advantages of each weight type, reflecting both objective data and subjective evaluator input on water resource vulnerability.

results.title: Weighting for what? A comparison of two weighting methods for measuring urban competitiveness - ScienceDirect
results.content: Using a hierarchical indicator system that considers economic, social, and environmental dimensions of the competitiveness of Chinese cities as a case study, it shows that principal component analysis (PCA) produces rankings of urban competitiveness that are significantly different from the alternative equal weighting (EW) method. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: the next section introduces the concept of urban competitiveness; the third section discusses the indicator system and the weighting methods for benchmarking the urban competitiveness of Chinese cities; the fourth section examines the impact different weighting methods have on the results of urban competitiveness evaluation and the fifth section gives the conclusions of this study. Based on a notion of competitiveness that takes into account the economic, social, and environmental dimensions, this paper has examined the impact that different weighting methods have on urban competitiveness rankings using data from Chinese cities.
